violated_invariant: A pool's base/quote token addresses must be fixed after deployment; init() must not be callable again (and never by an arbitrary caller) once the pool holds funds.
notes: The exploited contract is the DODO DVM pool 0x051ebd..., whose init() had no initialized guard; inside the flashLoan callback the attacker re-ran init() with two fake tokens so the repayment check measured balances of the fake tokens while the real wCRES/USDT left the pool. Its source was not recovered, and the three recovered candidates (wCRES WrappedERC20, a Gnosis Safe proxy used as maintainer, FeeRateModel) are not the defect location, so no Slither finding can explain the exploit; function names in locations are taken from the PoC call and public DODO code, not from recovered source.

violated_invariant: The NFT contract's init() must run exactly once (by the deployer); ownership and mint/burn rights must not be claimable by an arbitrary caller after deployment.
notes: The 88mph NFT contract's init(owner, name, symbol) was never called after deployment (or lacked an effective guard), so anyone could call it and become owner, then burn and re-mint existing token ids. No source was recovered for the victim and no Slither findings exist, so there is nothing to adjudicate; the file:function names are inferred from the PoC interface, not from recovered source.

violated_invariant: A relayed cross-chain message must never be able to target the bridge's own privileged contracts (EthCrossChainData) or invoke arbitrary selectors from the manager's privileged context; the keeper public key set must only change through the intended governance path.
notes: The defect is in EthCrossChainManager (no source recovered): _executeCrossChainTx let a verified message target any contract, including the manager-owned EthCrossChainData, with a selector derived from a user-chosen method string, so a brute-forced 4-byte collision for putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes replaced the keeper set; the attacker then signed fake unlock messages for LockProxy. EthCrossChainData and LockProxy have source but only contain the correctly-gated onlyOwner/onlyManagerContract code, so none of their findings explain the exploit. LockProxy arbitrary-send-eth [0] is by design behind onlyManagerContract, encode-packed-collision [26] is a false positive because every field is length-prefixed by WriteVarBytes, and uninitialized-local [76] is a struct whose fields are all assigned.

violated_invariant: msg.value may be credited at most once per transaction; a payable multicall that delegatecalls into payable commitEth must not let the same ETH be counted for every sub-call and then refunded from the contract's balance.
notes: The DutchAuction inherited a payable batch() that delegatecalls each encoded call, so five commitEth calls in one batch each saw the full msg.value and the overflow refund logic paid the excess out of the auction's own ETH. This is a design/logic flaw in composing a payable multicall with msg.value-dependent functions rather than a missing require, hence business_logic (input_validation would be the alternative). No source or findings were recovered for the auction contract; names are taken from the public MISO code.

violated_invariant: vVISR shares may only be minted in proportion to VISR actually received by the Hypervisor; the contract supplied as `from` must be a genuine Visor vault, not an arbitrary attacker contract whose owner() and delegatedTransferERC20() return whatever the caller wants.
notes: RewardsHypervisor.deposit accepts any `from` address, and when it is a contract it trusts IVisor(from).owner() == msg.sender and calls from.delegatedTransferERC20() with no check that `from` is a registered Visor vault or that any VISR arrived, so a fake vault minted 100M vVISR for free. The raw DHL label says reentrancy, but the PoC and code show no reentrant call; this is unvalidated trust in a caller-supplied contract. Slither's arbitrary-send-erc20 [0] is a real issue (anyone could pull VISR from an approved EOA via the else-branch) and sits in the same function, but it describes the safeTransferFrom branch, which has allowance protection, not the exploited delegatedTransferERC20 branch, so it does not explain the exploit; [16] is a harmless name shadowing.

violated_invariant: A contract that holds users' ERC20 allowances must never execute a caller-chosen call target with caller-chosen calldata; the exchange call must be restricted to a whitelisted 0x exchange and must not be able to invoke transferFrom on behalf of the writer.
notes: ACOWriter.write lets the caller pass exchangeAddress and exchangeData, and _sellACOTokens does _exchange.call(exchangeData) with no restriction, so with a mock ACO token the attacker made ACOWriter call USDC.transferFrom(victim, attacker, amount) using allowances users had granted to ACOWriter. Slither only reports an informational low-level-calls [4] on that exact call; it is a true statement about the dangerous line but the detector does not describe the weakness (user-controlled target and data), so it is valid but does not explain the exploit. The other findings are style, solc-version and constructor zero-checks.

violated_invariant: fnftsCreated (the next FNFT id) must be advanced before any external callback during a mint, so a reentrant depositAdditionalToFNFT cannot obtain the id of the FNFT series currently being minted and attach a deposit amount to it.
notes: FNFTHandler.mint calls ERC1155 _mint (which invokes onERC1155Received on the recipient) before incrementing fnftsCreated; during the callback for the 360000-unit series the attacker called depositAdditionalToFNFT on the earlier FNFT, whose getNextId() still returned the id of the series being minted, so one 1e18 deposit was recorded as the per-unit amount for all 360000 units, which were then withdrawn. Slither reentrancy-benign [46] names exactly that function, that external call and 'fnftsCreated += 1' written after it, which is the exploited weakness despite the 'benign' label, so it explains the exploit. [45] is the same ordering bug in mintBatchRec (real, not the path used), [58] is a genuine tautology, and [47] (reentrancy-eth in doMint via trusted WETH) is noise.

violated_invariant: Voting power used to pass and execute a BIP must not be obtainable within a single transaction; an emergency commit path that executes arbitrary diamondCut/init code needs a timelock or snapshot-based voting so flash-loaned Stalk cannot reach the supermajority.
notes: The attacker proposed a BIP whose init contract transfers the Silo's assets, waited the 24-hour emergencyCommit delay, then flash-loaned ~$1B of stables to mint BEAN3CRV, deposited it for instantly-counted Stalk, and called emergencyCommit, which executed the proposal via the diamond's init delegatecall. The defect is in the GovernanceFacet (vote weight from current deposits, no timelock on the emergency path), which is not among the recovered candidates; the recovered Diamond proxy, LibDiamond and Bean token are only forwarding/affected code, so no finding can explain the exploit. Diamond unused-state [37] is a false positive: AppStorage s is the diamond's shared storage anchor used by the facets.

violated_invariant: A borrower's accountBorrows must be recorded before any value is sent to the borrower; while a borrow is in flight the borrower must not be able to call Comptroller.exitMarket and withdraw the collateral backing that borrow.
notes: borrowFresh sends the borrowed ETH via Fuse's CEther.doTransferOut (to.call.value with unlimited gas) before writing accountBorrows; in the receive() hook the attacker called Comptroller.exitMarket, which read a zero borrow balance and released the fUSDC collateral, which was then redeemed. The CEtherDelegator candidate bundles the logic source, so its findings apply. reentrancy-no-eth [430] flags exactly this function, the accountBorrows writes after an external call and the cross-function reentrancy through borrowBalanceStoredInternal that exitMarket relied on, so it explains the exploit, with the caveat that Slither attributes the external call to the comptroller hooks because doTransferOut is abstract at the CToken level and it never sees the ETH send; confidence is medium for that reason. [397] and [434] are the same ordering issue seen through totalBorrows and the borrowInternal wrapper; [427]/[433] about the nonReentrant helper are noise.

violated_invariant: The proxy's own state (proxyAdmin) must not share storage slot 0 with the implementation's Initializable flags; initialize() on Governance, Staking and DelegateManager must be callable only once and never by an arbitrary caller after deployment.
notes: AudiusAdminUpgradeabilityProxy declares `address private proxyAdmin` as an ordinary state variable (slot 0) while the implementations inherit OpenZeppelin Initializable whose `initialized`/`initializing` booleans also live in slot 0; the second-lowest byte of the admin address made `initializing` read as true, so the initializer modifier always passed and the attacker re-initialized Governance (registry = self, votingPeriod 3, quorum 1%, guardian = self), Staking and DelegateManagerV2, gave himself 1e31 delegated stake and passed a proposal transferring AUDIO out of the governance treasury. The Governance logic candidate 0x1c91af... was deployed at block 15203848, after the fork block 15201793, so it is post-patch and excluded; pre-patch Governance code is present inside the flattened Staking/DelegateManagerV2 bundles. No Slither detector models proxy-vs-implementation layout, so nothing explains the exploit; the ______gap shadowing-state findings are the standard OZ upgradeable gap pattern and are false positives, while the proxy's missing zero-checks are real but minor.

violated_invariant: Only proposals genuinely approved by the DAO's Reality oracle process may be executed through the Safe module; the bond requirement and dispute window must make a bogus answer uneconomic.
notes: The Gnosis SafeSnap-style DaoModule lets anyone add a proposal and, because the module was deployed with a zero minimum bond (the `minBond == 0 ||` branch in executeProposalWithIndex skips the bond check) and only a 24h cooldown, the attacker answered their own Reality question with a 1 wei bond and executed mint/transferOwnership calls through the Safe. This is a governance-design/parameter weakness in otherwise standard module code rather than a classic coding error; the two timestamp findings (18, 19) sit in the execution path but flag block.timestamp use, not the missing bond/dispute protection, so nothing explains the exploit. Other candidates (RNBW, LPOP, PrimaryBridge, Realitio) are affected targets or the oracle, not the defect.

violated_invariant: Only an authorised minter may increase the token supply.
notes: Token.mint() is public with no modifier or caller check and mints a fixed 1e17 units to msg.sender, so the attacker simply called it and dumped the tokens into the Uniswap V3 pool. The only finding on mint() is too-many-digits (index 4), which comments on the literal, not the missing access control, so it does not explain the exploit; the remaining findings are dead inlined-OpenZeppelin code and compiler-version noise. The two UniswapV3Pool candidates are the drained venues, not defects.

violated_invariant: Redeeming N vault shares may pay out at most N shares' pro-rata portion of vault assets, with decimals/price state read from the slots the logic was written against.
notes: The victim address is a TransparentUpgradeableProxy and only the proxy/OZ sources were recovered; the exploited logic lives in the upgraded EFVault implementation, whose storage layout shifted relative to the proxy's existing state so the share-to-asset conversion in redeem() read a wrong (decimals/price) slot and paid ~5.1M USDC for 676,562 shares. The location names are taken from the PoC and public analyses, not from recovered source, hence medium confidence. All 36 proxy findings are OpenZeppelin library noise except the shadowing-local on the wrapper constructor (21), which is harmless; none touches the implementation, so nothing can explain a storage-layout bug Slither would need the implementation (and its upgrade history) to see.

violated_invariant: yUSDT share price must reflect only USDT-denominated holdings in the configured lending venues; a vault's constant iToken address must be the one matching its underlying.
notes: The legacy yUSDT iEarn vault was deployed with the Fulcrum address pointing at iUSDC rather than iUSDT, so its balance/share-price accounting counted a token it should never hold; the attacker used flash loans and Aave repayments to steer the APR recommender, donated iUSDC to inflate the share price, withdrew the real USDT, rebalanced the emptied vault and then minted huge yUSDT against 1 wei, dumping it into the Curve y-pool. I label the defect as a misconfigured constant (`other`) with a secondary business-logic failure (share price derived from manipulable/donated balances). The prepared file contains only the Aave debtor addresses with no source, so there are no Slither findings to adjudicate; victim_addresses is the yUSDT address from the PoC.

violated_invariant: Only the project owner may move a third party's token balance or call an arbitrary router with the contract's tokens; a user's balance may only decrease through transfers they authorise.
notes: VINU.addLiquidityETH is external and unrestricted: it takes caller-chosen router, LP-receiver and `devaddr` arguments, moves 80% of `devaddr`'s balance into the token contract, then calls the caller's router. The attacker passed the Uniswap pair as devaddr with a dummy router, repeatedly stripped VINU out of the pair, synced the reserves and sold into the distorted price. The two unused-return findings (11, 12) are on the defective function but describe ignored router/approve return values, not the missing access control or untrusted address parameters, so they do not explain the exploit; they, the shadowing-local pair and the reentrancy-no-eth on _transfer (external call to an owner-set router before balance updates) are real but minor. The UniswapV2Pair candidate is the affected venue; its findings are left unresolved.

violated_invariant: The omnipool's LP exchange rate must value its Curve LP positions at a price consistent with the price at which it actually adds/removes liquidity in the same transaction, so a deposit-then-withdraw round trip cannot extract value.
notes: The crvUSD omnipool mints and burns its LP token at an exchange rate computed from controller.priceOracle().getUSDPrice(curveLpToken) in _curveLpToUnderlying, while the actual Curve add/remove liquidity executes at the pools' current (attacker-skewed) balances; by flash-borrowing crvUSD, pushing the crvUSD/USDC and crvUSD/USDT pools off peg and sandwiching deposit/withdraw cycles the attacker turned the gap between oracle valuation and execution value into profit. The oracle contract itself is not among the candidates, so medium confidence on the exact split of blame. None of the 316 findings concerns oracle trust: the reentrancy-balance hits on depositFor/withdraw (255-258) flag ERC20 transfers of crvUSD, which has no hooks, and the incorrect-equality/uninitialized-local/unused-return hits are the usual `== 0` guard, memory-struct and mint/burn-return noise, so none explains the exploit.

violated_invariant: An account can withdraw at most what it (or its alt) actually deposited; alt-account withdrawals must debit the correct balance and never create withdrawable credit out of nothing.
notes: From the PoC alone: the attacker deposits 2 USDT/USDC, has a helper contract call lockTokens(attacker, 0) to register the attacker as its alt account, then calls withdrawTokensWithAlt(token, helper, 1e6), after which the helper can call withdrawTokens for the contract's entire token balance. That pattern indicates the alt-account withdrawal path mis-credits or fails to debit balances (a bookkeeping bug combined with unchecked alt/lock parameters) rather than a missing owner check. The victim contract has no recovered source and no Slither output, so no findings can be adjudicated and confidence is low on the exact defect line.

violated_invariant: When a swap moves the price exactly onto or across an initialised tick boundary, that tick must be crossed and the liquidity range updated; the swap-step arithmetic must not let the computed price land a hair short of the boundary while the quantities assume it was reached.
notes: The attacker flash-loaned, drove the pool price into a thin range, minted a concentrated position and then swapped so that the step arithmetic in SwapMath (computeSwapStep/calcReachAmount/calcFinalPrice) produced a final sqrt price just short of the tick boundary while the quantities were computed as if it had been reached; Pool.swap's boundary check therefore skipped the tick crossing, liquidity was double-counted and the pool paid out far more than it held. Slither's divide-before-multiply and incorrect-exp hits (13-22) are the well-known false positives on FullMath.mulDiv's modular-inverse and TickMath's fixed-point ladder, not the tick-crossing precision flaw in SwapMath/Pool.swap, so none explains the exploit. The reentrancy-no-eth and uninitialized-local hits are noise (trusted oracle calls, memory structs). The AntiSnipAttackPositionManager candidate is periphery, not the defect.

violated_invariant: collectInterest may only pull interest from registered staking contracts, and no external call made during interest collection may re-enter the reserve's buy/sell path before the collection's accounting completes.
notes: GoodFundManager.collectInterest takes a caller-supplied array of staking contracts and calls collectUBIInterest on each without checking they are registered; the attacker's fake staking contract re-entered the GoodReserve (GDX) buy path during that callback, after flash-loaning WETH and borrowing cDAI, so G$ were bought/minted at a stale reserve state and later sold back for DAI. Only the ERC1967 proxy/ProxyFactory1967 source was recovered for the victim (and for the reserve 0xa150...), not the GoodFundManager implementation, so the function names come from the PoC and public analyses. Every finding on the proxy candidate concerns the factory's assembly, naming and events and has nothing to do with the forwarded logic, so none explains the exploit; the GoodDollar token, cETH, cDAI and Unitroller candidates are affected third-party contracts and their findings are left unresolved.

violated_invariant: Only the holder of (or an account authorised for) the vault's BUI SetToken shares may redeem them, and redemption proceeds must go to that holder, not an arbitrary receiver.
notes: The PoC's whole attack is one call: redeem(BUI.balanceOf(victim), attacker) on the unverified SoulMate contract, which burns the contract's entire BUI SetToken holding and sends the underlying USDC/DAI/MATIC/AAVE/ENS/ZRX/UNI to the caller-chosen receiver, so the defect is a missing caller/ownership check on redeem with an unvalidated receiver. The victim has no recovered source, so no Slither output exists for it; the SetToken, Matic, Aave proxy, ENS and ZRX candidates are the redeemed basket and its components (third-party, not the defect), so their findings are left unresolved. Medium rather than high because the exact internal logic of redeem is inferred from the transaction effect, not read.

violated_invariant: Only the game's own settlement logic (not an arbitrary caller) may credit step income to a player; a player's claimable balance must be bounded by funds actually earned.
notes: MainPool.calcStepIncome is public with no caller check, so anyone can credit themselves stepIncome up to playBiggertReward and then drain it through withdraw; the PoC calls it directly after joining. Slither has no detector for a missing authorization check, and none of the MainPool findings touch calcStepIncome, so nothing explains the exploit. The uninitialized-local hits are zero-default locals and the naming/digit findings are noise.

violated_invariant: Collateral and borrow values fed into the account-liquidity check must be expressed in the same units for every market regardless of token decimals, so a borrow can never exceed the collateral factor times true collateral value.
notes: With 1 WETH of collateral the attacker borrowed OHM (9 dec), USDC (6 dec) and WBTC (8 dec) worth about $1.4M, which only works if the price fed to the liquidity check was normalized inconsistently across token decimals; public write-ups describe a price-normalization/decimals error in the lending stack. The Comptroller candidate's math is stock Compound and the mis-scaled price comes from the external oracle, which is not among the recovered candidates, so the defect contract is not in the Slither set and no finding describes it. boolean-cst/boolean-equal and naming findings are Compound-style noise.

violated_invariant: A contract that holds user token approvals must never execute caller-supplied calldata against a caller-chosen target, otherwise anyone can spend those approvals via transferFrom.
notes: The PoC sends a crafted aggregator call whose embedded payload is DMTR.transferFrom(victim, aggregator, balance), so the aggregator implementation forwards attacker-chosen target+calldata and spends approvals users gave it. Only the OpenZeppelin proxy source was recovered; the implementation is unverified, so the defect function is not in the Slither set and every recovered finding is dependency-library noise about the proxy, not the exploit.

violated_invariant: initialize() on an upgradeable (UUPS) contract must be callable only once by the deployer, so ownership and the upgrade right can never be claimed by an outsider.
notes: The PoC simply calls initialize() on the live proxy to become owner, then upgradeToAndCall to a malicious implementation that sends the ETH balance out, which is the classic unprotected initializer. No source was recovered for the proxy or implementation, so there are no Slither findings to adjudicate.

violated_invariant: No pool reserve may be driven to zero by a liquidity removal, and a swap must never pay out more than the constant-product price implies; with x=0 the x*y=k formula degenerates and pays the whole output reserve for one wei.
notes: The attacker used flash-loaned capital to own almost all LP via addMultiple, then removeLiquidity for ETH: (1-R)^16 in 0.64 fixed point rounds to exactly zero, so the pool pays out its entire ETH balance and the reserve becomes 0; swap() then computes netInput*outBal/((0<<64)+netInput) = the whole output reserve for a 1-wei input, and chaining 1-wei swaps drained every token. This is derived from the recovered code and the PoC call sequence rather than a confirmed post-mortem, hence medium confidence. Slither failed to compile the DeFiPlaza candidate (absolute source path), so there are zero findings to adjudicate.

violated_invariant: A router that users approve must restrict which targets/selectors a command may call so a caller cannot make it invoke token.transferFrom on another user's allowance.
notes: The PoC calls the Spectra router's execute(commands, inputs) with command 0x12 whose input encodes target=asdCRV and calldata transferFrom(victim, attacker, balance); the router executes it with its own approval from the victim, so the defect is an unvalidated external call in the router implementation. Only the proxy/admin source was recovered (implementation missing), so the defect function is absent from the Slither set and the recovered findings are OpenZeppelin proxy noise.

violated_invariant: Rewards paid to a staker must be proportional to the principal actually withdrawn and must be marked as claimed, so repeated partial withdrawals cannot pay the full reward each time.
notes: withdraw(_amount) pays getPendingRewards(), which is the full reward on every matured deposit, regardless of how much is withdrawn and without ever resetting it; the PoC withdraws 1 wei 800 times after the 14-day vest and receives the full reward each call. None of the sorraStaking findings describe this: the two reentrancy-benign hits are on nonReentrant functions calling a trusted extension and the timestamp warnings are ordinary vesting comparisons, so they are false positives, and no detector flags the reward-accounting flaw.

violated_invariant: A permissionless function that swaps protocol-held tokens must enforce a bounded slippage against a manipulation-resistant price; an unbounded caller-supplied slippage override lets anyone sandwich the swap.
notes: depositFromPairedLpToken is public and takes _slippageOverride with no upper bound; the attacker flash-swapped pOHM, skewed the pOHM/PEAS V3 pool, called it with slippage 999 so amountOutMinimum was ~0.1% of the TWAP quote, and the contract dumped its pOHM into the manipulated pool before the attacker swapped back. Slither's hits on this function (divide-before-multiply, reentrancy-no-eth, unused-return) describe other patterns in the same body, not the unbounded slippage or the manipulable execution price, so none explain the exploit; the uninitialized-local on _adminAmt is a deliberate zero default.

violated_invariant: Collateral used to back a borrow must be valued by a price that cannot be moved within the same transaction by the borrower.
notes: The PoC flash-borrows WETH, pumps AMP across three pools, posts the AMP as Kashi collateral and borrows USDC in the same transaction, which is only possible if the pair's solvency check used an oracle that reflected the pumped price. The Kashi pair clone and its oracle were not recovered, so the defect code is not in the Slither set; BentoBox is only the share vault. The arbitrary-send-erc20 hit on BentoBoxV1.deposit is a false positive because deposit() is gated by the allowed() master-contract approval check.

off_chain_reason: designed_protocol_behavior: Liquity-v2 urgentRedemption on a shut-down branch pays redeemers a collateral bonus by design; the $4.2k is that bonus captured with flash-loaned USDaf, not a code defect
violated_invariant: None at the code level: after branch shutdown any USDaf holder is intended to be able to redeem debt for collateral at a small premium so the branch winds down.
notes: The PoC mints USDaf from flash-loaned USDT and calls TroveManager.urgentRedemption on two chosen troves of the shut-down scrvUSD branch, taking collateral with the protocol's intended redemption bonus; the ActivePool only releases collateral on the TroveManager's instruction. This is designed wind-down behavior rather than a bug, so I mark it out of scope (medium confidence: if the shutdown itself was triggered by a faulty price feed that would be a separate defect in a contract not among the candidates). The reentrancy-no-eth hits in ActivePool are mint calls to the trusted BOLD token and are false positives; nothing explains an exploit here.

violated_invariant: Tokens may only be pulled from `from` if `from` actually authorized the router (via a real permit or its own call); a no-op permit on an attacker-supplied token's underlying must not authorize transferFrom of a third party's approval.
notes: The router takes an attacker-chosen `token`, reads its underlying (WETH), calls permit on it, and then transferFrom(from, ...) using whatever allowance `from` had already granted the router; WETH has no permit, its fallback swallows the call, so the signature is never checked. Finding 0 (arbitrary-send-erc20-permit) names exactly this: an arbitrary `from` in transferFrom combined with a permit call in anySwapOutUnderlyingWithPermit, the exploited function, so it qualifies. Findings 1 and 2 flag the same pattern in the two sibling functions that were not used but share the weakness.

violated_invariant: A swap must never decrease the stable-pool invariant D beyond fees; rounding in balance upscaling and in the amount-out path must favor the pool, not the trader, even when a balance has been pushed to a few wei.
notes: The attacker uses batch swaps to drive one token balance down to a handful of wei, where the round-down in _upscale/_swapGivenOut (balances and amountOut scaled with mulDown) makes the computed invariant D drop relative to real balances, so BPT and the other tokens can be bought cheaply and the pool unwound at a profit. No Slither finding touches StableMath, BaseGeneralPool or the scaling helpers; the 44 divide-before-multiply hits are all in the LogExpMath library, which is unrelated to the stable invariant path, so nothing explains the exploit. The uninitialized-local and unused-return hits on the pool contracts are deliberate patterns, so I marked them invalid; the rest are left unresolved. The two pool candidates share the same source, so the same indices apply to both.

violated_invariant: The vault's USDC-to-WETH conversion must execute at a fair price (minimum-out / TWAP), and must not be triggerable by an arbitrary caller who has just moved the spot price of the pool it swaps through.
notes: The PoC flash-loans USDC, skews the USDC/WETH V3 pool, calls the permissionless vault.swapToWETH(100k USDC) which swaps at the manipulated price with no slippage floor, then reverses the pool and keeps the difference. The vault contract 0x6a06... has no recovered source (sourcify not_found) and the only candidates with Slither output are third-party contracts (Morpho, OKX DexRouter, TokenApprove, the Uniswap pool) that are not the defect, so there is nothing to adjudicate; the function name comes from the PoC interface, not verified source.

violated_invariant: An authorized signature must bind every field that determines what the strategy will approve and call (fromToken, toToken, amount, aggregator), not only the calldata bytes.
notes: _validateAuthorization hashes only keccak256(swap.data) for each SwapInfo, so the signer's approval does not cover fromToken/toToken/amount/aggregator; the attacker reuses a valid signature with aggregator set to their own contract and amount = max, and executeSwap then forceApproves the gauge token to that aggregator and calls it. Slither has no detector for incomplete EIP-712 coverage; the reentrancy-balance hits (99-102) on executeSwap flag the external call but describe reentrancy, not the missing signature binding, so none explains. The timestamp and uninitialized-local hits at the defect function are noise (a deadline comparison and a bytes variable that is appended to).

violated_invariant: The router may only transferFrom the account that initiated the current lock; the payer in payCallback must be derived from the caller, not from attacker-supplied payload data.
notes: The exploited contract is the Ekubo EVM router (0x8ccb...), whose payCallback accepted a payer address from the lock payload and called transferFrom on it, so any address with a standing WBTC approval to the router could be drained by looping core.lock (85 times, 0.2 WBTC each). The router has no recovered source, and the PoC replaces it with a readable stand-in, so the function names are reconstructed; Ekubo Core (which has source) only forwards lock/pay callbacks and is not the defect, so I did not adjudicate its findings.

violated_invariant: A rollup proof accepted by escapeHatch must cryptographically bind the withdrawals paid out by processDepositsAndWithdrawals to valid, previously deposited notes; value cannot leave the rollup except for what the circuit constrains.
notes: The permissionless escapeHatch forwards a caller-built proof to the external TurboVerifier (0x48cb..., not a candidate) with rollupSize taken from the proof; the verifier accepted a proof whose public withdrawal inputs were not bound by the deployed escape-hatch verification key, and the processor then paid out the rollup's ETH/DAI/renBTC to the attacker. The defect is in the proof system / verifier key and the processor's trust of proof-decoded outputs, which no Slither detector can model; the arbitrary-send-eth and reentrancy hits on withdraw describe the payout mechanics, not the broken validation, so none explains. Confidence is low because the real flaw lives outside the recovered Solidity.

violated_invariant: The factory must only issue initializePool/mint calls to the PositionManager on behalf of the new launch; caller-supplied calldata executed with the factory as msg.sender must not be able to change approvals or touch other launches' positions.
notes: launch() is permissionless and passes initCalldata and modifyCalldata verbatim into PositionManager.multicall with the factory as msg.sender, so the attacker substituted setApprovalForAll(attacker, true) and then burned every factory-owned LP position. Slither reports unused-return (53) and reentrancy-benign on that exact multicall line, but those describe ignoring a return value / event ordering, not the forwarding of unvalidated calldata to an external contract, so none explains; the arbitrary-send-eth hit is the intended dust refund to msg.sender. The unchecked-transfer hits are genuine (raw transfer on arbitrary paired tokens), the uninitialized-local hits are accumulators intentionally starting at zero.

violated_invariant: A registry's initialize() must be callable once, by the deployer only; the manager that controls which implementation item-adapter clones delegatecall into must not be replaceable by an arbitrary caller.
notes: Both live contract registries exposed an unprotected initialize(uint256) that re-set the pending manager, so the attacker re-ran it, accepted manager, registered their own code as the body for the item adapters' transfer selectors, pulled 54 items from holders without approval and melted them for ENJ. Neither registry nor the platform has recovered source (only the ENJ token, which is not the defect), so function names are taken from the PoC interface and there are no Slither findings to adjudicate.

violated_invariant: transfer(to, x) called by a counterparty that means 'x wei' must move x wei; a token whose transfer silently re-interprets small values as NFT ids and moves a full unit breaks the accounting of any AMM holding it.
notes: O404.transfer treats any valueOrId <= maxTotalSupplyERC721 (50) as an NFT id and moves a full 1e18 units plus the NFT; a Uniswap V3 exact-output swap for `id` wei makes the pool call transfer(attacker, id) and hand over 1e18 O404 while only debiting a few wei, after the attacker arranged (via pool.flash repaid by id-path transfers) for the pool to own the low ids. Slither's erc721-interface hits (7-10) complain that approve/transferFrom return bool, which is the ERC-404 hybrid by design and says nothing about the id/amount overloading, so none explains and I marked them invalid. The dual interpretation is inherent ERC-404 v1 design, but it is a code-level logic flaw when the token whitelists an AMM pool, so it stays in scope.

violated_invariant: Interest for an idle period must be accrued once, at the utilization that held during that period; a depositor who arrives after the gap must not earn the whole gap's deposit interest at a utilization they set in the same block.
notes: _checkFirstAction stores the full 264k-block idle gap as inactiveActionDelta and freezes actionEXR on the block's first action, and the interest model (0x29ec..., not a candidate) then multiplies that whole gap by a rate computed from live totals on every later action in the block, so a flash-loaned deposit plus borrows to spike utilization credits ~36 days of interest that a repay/withdraw loop cashes out. Slither's unused-return hits (70, 85) sit on the exact setBlocks/syncActionEXR lines but only say a bool return is ignored, not that the gap is applied at manipulable utilization, so none explains. The proxy's controlled-delegatecall hits are false positives (fixed handler address and fixed selectors) and the reentrancy-balance hits on the ERC20 wrappers are noise. The logic contract 0x47be... is the handler the proxy delegates to; the proxy itself only forwards.
